source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? Theory of mind predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face
finding: Replication of the c factor with a new task battery. 68 groups randomly assigned face-to-face or online (text chat only). A single dominant first factor appeared in both.
numbers: First factor explained 49% of variance face-to-face (N=32 groups) and 41% online (N=36). Second factor under half of that. Pre-planned minimum 60 groups for 80% power.
limits: Same lab group as the original. Student/lab sample. Tasks were new, so this replicates the factor, not the exact battery.
agent_relevance: Shows c is not tied to one battery, but it is one lab. Background only.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? Theory of mind predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face
finding: Average Reading the Mind in the Eyes (RME) score of members predicted c equally well online and face-to-face, even with no visual cues.
numbers: RME with c: r=.53 (p=.002) face-to-face, r=.55 (p<.001) online. Without the two lowest-RME groups: r=.47 and r=.48 (both p<.01).
limits: Small N per condition (32 and 36). RME is an eye-photo test; the paper argues it proxies wider theory-of-mind skill.
agent_relevance: Social sensitivity effect survives text-only channels. For a text-only agent group, mentalizing about other agents may matter more than visual cues.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? Theory of mind predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face
finding: Participation distribution and amount of communication also predicted c, in both conditions. A personality general factor did not.
numbers: Proportion female with c: r=.41 (p=.01) online; RME mediated the female effect (Sobel z=1.95, p=.05). More communication went with higher c; SD of communication (domination) went with lower c. General factor of personality unrelated to c or RME (p>.05).
limits: Mediation test is marginal (p=.05). Correlational throughout; no manipulation of turn-taking.
agent_relevance: Dominance by one speaker lowers group output. Supports equal-voice protocols in multi-agent set-ups, as a hypothesis only.

source: Bates & Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: Evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence in the performance of human groups (Intelligence 60:46-56)
finding: Three studies (312 people) found a general group factor, but it was almost entirely explained by member IQ. This is the strongest challenge to the claim that c is independent of IQ.
numbers: Abstract: individual IQ accounted for about 80% of group-IQ differences. Study 1 (26 groups): single factor 39.8% of variance (adjusted eigenvalues 1.98, .85, .69, .69, .79); regression on IQ, RME, proportion female explained 57% of variance, only IQ significant (beta=.76, p<.001); RME beta=-.11 ns; proportion female beta=.12 ns.
limits: Study 1 used Raven for individual IQ and Raven items in one group task (overlap). Different participant samples (Scotland, India). Only 3 to 5 tasks per battery, fewer than Woolley.
agent_relevance: If group ability tracks member ability, a strong base model plus a scaffold may matter more than group process.

source: Bates & Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: Evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence in the performance of human groups (Intelligence 60:46-56)
finding: Study 2 (40 groups of 3, Chennai) and Study 3 (40 groups, Scotland) used the same Wonderlic IQ test as Woolley 2010. Group IQ was mostly average member IQ.
numbers: Studies 2 and 3 combined: average IQ alone accounted for 81% of group-IQ variance (beta .86, t=13.6). RME added beta=.19 (p=.019) in a linear model. Structural model with IQ path fixed at 1.0 and residual 0 fit with no loss (chi2 change=0, p=1.0; CFI=1.00; RMSEA=0). Model where RME drives group IQ fit badly (CFI=.60).
limits: Participants educated to undergraduate level and fluent in English; authors rebut range restriction (Wonderlic mean 17.07, SD 7.4). Raffle incentive is weak.
agent_relevance: Group ability may reduce to average member ability. For LLM groups, the base model strength dominates.

source: Bates & Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: Evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence in the performance of human groups (Intelligence 60:46-56)
finding: Failed replication of the gender and turn-taking effects. All-male, all-female and mixed groups performed equally.
numbers: Proportion female not significant in any of three studies (Study 3 polynomial terms p=.29, .12, .72). Turn-taking variance not related to group IQ. Authors call the original findings likely false positives. Original reported r=.23 (p=.007) with proportion female.
limits: Turn-taking was measured in small groups of 3 and without sociometric badges, so a weaker test.
agent_relevance: Do not design agent groups around gender or exact turn-taking quotas. These levers did not replicate.

source: Bates & Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: Evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence in the performance of human groups (Intelligence 60:46-56)
finding: Intervention test inside Study 3 (40 groups): telling groups to be empathic, or to obey the smartest member, did not help.
numbers: Empathy, authority and control groups (14, 12, 14): F(2,34)=1.14, p=.33. Authority beta=-.42 (p=.14), empathy beta=-.13 (p=.62), both negative. Several groups hit ceiling on the Raven task.
limits: Run after the main study as an add-on; ceiling effect weakens power; authors place little emphasis on it.
agent_relevance: A plain instruction to be empathic did not raise group output. Process instructions in prompts may need more than a sentence.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cogn Res Princ Implic 6:26)
finding: Meta-analysis of c versus criterion tasks. c predicts later group performance moderately, but average member IQ was rarely controlled.
numbers: c with criterion task: r=.26 (95% CI .10 to .40), 8 independent samples, 9 tasks, N=857 groups. Subset with IQ (5 samples, N=366 groups): average member IQ with performance r=.06 (95% CI -.08 to .20; I2=35%). Average IQ with c: r=.19 (K=5, n=345).
limits: Authors say about 80% of studies were underpowered. Mix of lab, field and unpublished theses. Overlapping authors in the original studies.
agent_relevance: Best single quantitative summary: c is a real but modest predictor; incremental validity over IQ is unproven.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cogn Res Princ Implic 6:26)
finding: The first factor is weaker than its headline variance share suggests. Total variance and average variance extracted differ.
numbers: First-factor share 43% and 44% in Woolley Studies 1 and 2. Average variance extracted (squared loadings) 30.23% over 49 loadings, range 22% (Woolley Study 2) to 37% (Bates and Gupta Studies 2 and 3 combined). Fornell-Larcker minimum recommended 50%. About 90% of between-task correlations positive (positive manifold, mean over studies).
limits: Their AVE reading is one view; defenders argue 30 to 50% matches individual-g batteries.
agent_relevance: Treat a 43% first factor as moderate g-like structure, not one strong trait.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cogn Res Princ Implic 6:26)
finding: Study-level means show the triple: c to criterion about .25, c to average IQ about .19, average IQ to criterion about .07. A small thesis sample was weaker still.
numbers: Mean effects .253, .185, .067 for c-criterion, IQ-c, IQ-criterion. Rowe 2019 thesis (29 groups): c-criterion r=.104 (p=.59), IQ-c r=.294 (p=.12), IQ-criterion r=.202 (p=.29).
limits: Means are unweighted across mixed designs; one criterion task per study; c was built from the same kind of tasks.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cogn Res Princ Implic 6:26)
finding: Most c studies are too small to settle small effects. The funnel plot showed no missing studies for c-criterion.
numbers: Of 19 samples only 6 (31.6%) had enough groups to detect r=.10 to .30 at 80% power; none had the 784 needed for r=.10. Nearly all exceeded the 29 groups needed for r=.50.
limits: Meta-level critique by independent authors, not a replication.
agent_relevance: A big preregistered multi-site test of c versus IQ is still missing. Treat any c-based design rule as provisional.

source: Graf, Gimpel, Barlow (2019) Clarifying the structure of collective intelligence in teams: a meta-analysis (Collective Intelligence conference abstract)
finding: Pooled correlations across task types gave no single factor. Meta-analytic structural equation modelling found three factors (idea generation, conflict resolution, task execution).
numbers: 745 teams, 13 studies, 6 papers. Pooled 5x5 correlation matrix across task types had average inter-task r=.001, entries from -.17 to .17. One-factor CFA bad: chi2=40.79, df=5, CFI=.73, TLI=.45, RMSEA=.10. First factor eigenvalue 1.05 (threshold 1.38) explaining 17%; second 15%. Parallel analysis: 3 factors.
limits: Short work-in-progress abstract. Pools by McGrath task type, which can dilute task-level structure. Only 5 of 8 task types covered. Not peer-reviewed in this form.
agent_relevance: Most direct evidence against one general factor. An agent benchmark should score separate group abilities, not one number.

source: Credé & Howardson (2017) The structure of group task performance: A second look at the evidence for the collective intelligence construct (J Appl Psychol 102:1483-1492)
finding: Reanalysis of six published samples. Says support for a general group factor is weak; low-effort responding and nesting may inflate small covariation.
numbers: Six samples reanalysed (per-sample numbers not read). Only the 2014 Indiana study correctly found no c, per press coverage.
limits: Known only from a search summary, not the paper. No effect sizes recorded.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: common effort variance mimics a factor.

source: ScienceDaily press summary of Credé & Howardson (2017)
finding: Press report names three artifact claims: conflicting data across studies, unmotivated or confused participants (low effort), and tasks where members' separate answers were averaged without real collaboration.
numbers: One example: in a brick-uses task a point per use regardless of practicality, with at least one team scoring zero. No numbers given.
limits: Secondary source, not peer-reviewed text.
agent_relevance: A c-like factor can arise from task engagement alone.

source: Woolley, Kim, Malone (2018) Measuring collective intelligence in groups: a reply to Credé and Howardson (SSRN 3187373)
finding: Authors reply that the data do not support the artifact reading, while agreeing that better measures of c are needed.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Could not open (HTTP 403). Known only from a search result summary.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (PNAS 118(21):e2005737118)
finding: Largest pro-c synthesis. A general CI factor holds in a 22-study meta-analysis. Group process predicts it most, then member skill, then composition.
numbers: 22 studies, 5,279 individuals, 1,356 groups. Proportion of women predicts group performance, mediated by social perceptiveness. CI predicts out-of-sample criterion tasks.
limits: Only the abstract (via Crossref) was read; the full text could not be fetched. Co-authors include Woolley and Malone, the original team.
agent_relevance: Pro-c side of the dispute; set against Rowe 2021 (r=.26, IQ not controlled) and Graf 2019 (3 factors).

source: Meslec, Aggarwal, Curseu (2016) The insensitive ruins it all: compositional and compilational influences of social sensitivity on collective intelligence (Front Psychol 7:676)
finding: Weak-link rule: the lowest social-sensitivity member predicts c better than the mean or the highest.
numbers: 30 Dutch student groups (3 to 6 members, mean 4.97), text chat, Engel battery (62 minutes). c with min RME r=.52 (p<.01), max RME r=.41, mean RME r=.48, group-version sensitivity r=.38. Regression: min RME beta=.49 (p<.05); max .19 ns; adjusted R2=.27. Mean excluding the minimum member not significant (beta=-.07).
limits: N=30 groups. Correlational. Minimum and mean are strongly correlated (r=.82).
agent_relevance: One socially blind or low-mentalising agent may drag the group. Suggests checking the weakest member of an agent team.

source: Janssens, Meslec, Leenders (2022) Collective intelligence in teams: contextualizing collective intelligent behavior over time (Front Psychol 13:989572)
finding: Review of the c research stream. Argues CI lives in interaction processes over time, not only in outcome scores. Its Table 1 summarises replications.
numbers: Table 1: Woolley Study 2 152 groups; Engel 2014 32 and 36; Engel 2015 68, 25 (German students), 116 (Japanese organisations); Barlow and Dennis 86 (no c in computer-mediated groups); Bates and Gupta 26, 40, 40; Kim 2017 248 League of Legends teams (c predicted later play).
limits: Review and position paper; no new data. Table is the authors' own summary.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions: c reported across cultures and an online game, not in Barlow and Dennis. Process data over time is the proposed next step.

source: Barlow & Dennis (2016) Not as smart as we think (J Manage Inf Syst 33(3):684-712), as reported by Rowe 2021 and Janssens 2022
finding: Failed replication of a general factor in computer-mediated groups. Rowe notes the authors judged c not valid and did not apply it to their criterion task.
numbers: 86 virtual groups in the main study. A separate thesis experiment (65 groups) showed a c only in the experimental coordination-structuring group, with c-criterion r=.339 (p=.026).
limits: Second-hand: I did not open the original paper. Details of the intervention not verified.
agent_relevance: A structured coordination process may create c where free groups do not. Matches the idea of a scaffold, but is one thesis study.

source: Engel et al. (2015) Collective intelligence in computer-mediated collaboration emerges in different contexts and cultures (CHI), as listed in Janssens 2022
finding: Cross-cultural replication of c in online groups: US (68 groups), Germany (25 student groups), Japan (116 groups in organisations).
numbers: Sample sizes 68, 25, 116. As summarised by Janssens: c present across settings and media, correlated with performance on complex tasks.
limits: Second-hand only; original CHI paper not opened; variance explained not read.
agent_relevance: Cultural generalisation is claimed on small samples.

source: Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone (2024) When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: Preregistered meta-analysis of human-AI groups. On average they are worse than the best of human or AI alone. Gains only for creation tasks and when humans beat the AI.
numbers: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes. Overall Hedges g=-0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07). Decision tasks g=-0.27 (P=.002). Creation tasks g=0.19 (95% CI -0.09 to 0.48, ns, n=34). Combinations beat humans alone (augmentation) but not the best part (synergy).
limits: Studies from Jan 2020 to June 2023, mostly pre-LLM. Possible publication bias; varied designs. No c factor measured.
agent_relevance: Closest hard data on mixed human-AI group intelligence. Mixing a weaker partner can lower decision accuracy; match roles to who is stronger.

source: Riedl (2025/2026) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models (arXiv 2510.05174, ICLR 2026)
finding: Information-theoretic test for higher-order structure in LLM agent groups with no direct communication, in a group guessing game. Personas, and a prompt to think about what others might do, push groups from aggregates toward coordinated collectives.
numbers: Pilot: GPT-4.1, group sizes 3 to 15, 11 temperatures, 50 groups each (7,150 experiments). Each extra member cut odds of success about 8% (OR=0.92, p<1e-16); each unit of temperature raised odds about 50% (OR=1.50). Main: N=10, T=1, 200 groups per condition (Plain, Persona, Persona+ToM); overall success not different by condition. About 32% of groups showed significant emergence capacity (Plain 37%, Persona 44%, ToM 18%).
limits: Simple guessing game. No c factor or task battery measured. Models: GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1 8B and 70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3 235B; the 8B model showed little to no emergence.
agent_relevance: Group size hurts coordination in LLM groups as in human groups. Prompt-level role differentiation changes group structure.

source: Riedl (2025/2026) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models
finding: Performance gain needs both redundancy (shared goal alignment) and synergy (complementary roles). Either alone did not predict success.
numbers: Synergy x redundancy interaction beta=0.24 (p=.014); each amplifies the other's effect by 27% on the log-odds scale. Theory-of-mind prompt raises performance via synergy: ACME=0.034, 95% CI -0.000 to 0.07, p=.053 (marginal).
limits: Marginal mediation. Single task. Observational regression with inverse-probability weighting, not randomised on synergy.
agent_relevance: Echoes the human finding that theory of mind helps groups; here it works through complementary roles.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: which yields better decisions in multi-agent LLMs? (arXiv 2508.17536, NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight)
finding: In LLM agent groups, majority voting captures most of the gain credited to multi-agent debate. Debate alone adds no expected accuracy, since belief updates form a martingale.
numbers: 7 benchmarks, 2 models. Qwen2.5-7B average: single .7205, best decentralized debate (T=2) .7377, majority vote .7691. Llama3.1-8B: single .6203, best sparse debate .6990, majority vote .7242. Arithmetic with Qwen: single .8140, majority vote .9900, centralized debate .43 to .55.
limits: Small models (7B, 8B). Voting and debate use the same agents; no social-sensitivity or turn-taking manipulation. Authors show biasing updates toward correction can help debate.
agent_relevance: Aggregation beats free discussion unless discussion is tuned. Interaction quality, not size, is the lever, as in human c.

source: Li et al. (2026) Superminds Test: actively evaluating collective intelligence of agent society via probing agents (arXiv 2604.22452)
finding: A society of over two million LLM agents (MoltBook) showed no emergent collective intelligence on probes. Scale alone did not produce it.
numbers: Tier I, Humanity's Last Exam: 2,158 problems, 98.4% of posts got no comments; on the 35 commented posts the society scored 11.4% (individual) and 8.6% (joint), below frontier models at 14.3 to 20.0%. Of 111 comments, 76.5% superficial or irrelevant, 9.0% any substantive reasoning, 3.6% correct reasoning. Tier II: 93 of 103 distributed-premise math posts (90.3%) got no external comments. Tier III counting: 35 of 50 (70%) got no replies.
limits: Measures an open uncontrolled social platform, not assigned groups. Tiny commented subsets (n=35). Not a c-factor measure.
agent_relevance: Failure was non-interaction, not low ability. Matches the human claim that process, not member skill, drives c.

source: On the dynamics of multi-agent LLM communities driven by value diversity (arXiv 2512.10665, 2025)
finding: Pilot with Llama-3.1-70B agents. More agents and more diverse value profiles gave deeper discussion and better rules, with a plateau near 30 agents.
numbers: Group sizes 4, 10, 30; 25 rounds. Multi-value agents proposed 20 to 30% more high-quality rules than single-value agents. No statistical tests, effect sizes, or seed variance reported.
limits: Self-described pilot, single base model, undefined emergence index. No c factor measured; Woolley cited as motivation.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that diversity helps; do not rely on it.

source: Scofield (2026) Multi-agent constraint factorization reveals latent invariant solution structure (arXiv 2601.15077)
finding: Theory: agents each enforcing their own constraints converge to the intersection of constraint sets, which a single agent applying all constraints at once generally cannot reach.
numbers: No experimental numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. No collective-intelligence-factor content; thematic link only.
agent_relevance: A formal route to why decomposed roles can beat one agent; untested empirically here.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330:686-688), numbers as reported by Engel 2014, Bates 2017 and Rowe 2021
finding: Founding study, read only second-hand (Science page returned 403). A single factor explained 43 to 44% of variance in group scores; c predicted later hard-task performance better than average or maximum member IQ.
numbers: Study 1: 40 groups, first factor 43% (a priori rule 30 to 50%, eigenvalue above 1.38). Study 2: 152 groups, first factor 44%. Proportion female with c r=.23 (p=.007), per Bates. RME effect on group IQ controlling for individual IQ about .36 in the largest study, per Bates.
limits: Not read directly. Rowe computes Study 2 average variance extracted at 22%.
agent_relevance: Sets the bar. Later work (Bates, Rowe, Graf) weakens the independence from IQ.
